wine.name: Georges de Latour Private Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, nearly all of it, with a little Petit Verdot and, in some years, a touch of Malbec or Merlot.
wine.sites: BV Ranch No. 1 and BV Ranch No. 2 on the Rutherford bench, on the west side of the valley floor, vineyards the founder first planted in the early 1900s.
wine.making: Part of the crop is fermented in new French oak barrels and the rest in stainless steel and concrete tanks; the malolactic fermentation and the ageing follow in barrel, about twenty months or more in French oak, nearly all of it new. For decades it was aged in American oak, until French barrels came in around 1990.
wine.glass: Cassis, black cherry and cedar over dried sage and cocoa, with the dry, dusty grip André Tchelistcheff called Rutherford dust; firm, fine grained tannin, fresh acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it opens after ten years or so in a strong vintage and can last for decades, as the old vintages tasted long after release have shown.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The founder of Beaulieu, who died in 1940; the wine bears his name, not that of another estate.
First the family's own lot of 1936, released for sale under the founder's name, and the house's leading Cabernet ever since.
The appellation on the label; the grapes grow at Rutherford, within it.

records.table: Rutherford dust was André Tchelistcheff's name for the dry, dusty grip of Cabernet from the Rutherford bench, and Beaulieu Vineyard's Georges de Latour Private Reserve, which he shaped for decades, is where to taste it. First made in 1936, it pairs that grip with cassis and cedar.
records.story: Georges de Latour, a Frenchman, and his wife bought their first land at Rutherford in 1900; on seeing it, the house says, she called it a beau lieu, a beautiful place, and the name stayed. Through Prohibition, by the house's account, Beaulieu kept its cellar working by making wine for the altars of the Catholic Church. In 1938 de Latour brought André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), a Russian born winemaker he had met in France, to Rutherford. Tasting the family's private lot of 1936 Cabernet Sauvignon, Tchelistcheff urged that it be bottled and sold as the house's flagship, and it was released about 1940, the year de Latour died, under his name. Tchelistcheff stayed some three decades, coined the phrase Rutherford dust for the dry, dusty grip of the bench's Cabernet and trained a generation of Napa winemakers. In 1969 the family sold Beaulieu to the Heublein company, and the house has since passed through several drinks groups. For decades the Private Reserve was aged in American oak; French barrels came in around 1990 and have since taken over. Its long run of vintages links Napa before the Second World War to the valley's later Cabernet.

Tchelistcheff advised many wineries after he left, but Beaulieu was the house where he made wine for some three decades.

Georges de Latour's year of birth, 1856, stood only in a college course page and a blog, so he is dated by his death in 1940 (Vinous, the Napa Wine Project) and not given a span.

Tchelistcheff's end at Beaulieu is 1973 in one account and 1968 in another, so the story says some three decades; his dates rest on Wikipedia and the Wine History Project, and match the refuted Ornellaia record.

The blend, the vessels and the barrel time are drawn from the house's sheets for the vintages 2015 to 2023, which give twenty to twenty four months in French oak, ninety or more per cent new; the American oak until 1989 is Decanter's.
Prohibition's altar wine is the house's account alone, so it is hedged; the 1923 purchase of a neighbour's stone winery, on the house's word alone, is left out.
The library's w-georges-de-latour-private-reserve calls it the longest running reserve Cabernet in Napa; that claim of a first was not tested and the record does not make it.

The first release of the 1936: 1940 in most accounts met and on the house's history page, 1941 on another house page; about 1940 stays.

records.place: St Helena, with the vineyard at Oakville, Napa Valley, California

wine.name: Martha's Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, from the one vineyard.
wine.sites: Martha's Vineyard, on the well drained western bench of Oakville, with eucalyptus trees along its edge. Heitz agreed in 1965, on a handshake, to buy all its Cabernet from the couple who had bought the land in 1963.
wine.making: After fermentation the wine spends about a year in large, neutral oak tanks, then moves to new barrels of French Limousin oak. It is bottled after years in wood and held a further year in bottle at the winery before release, a regime that has varied from vintage to vintage.
wine.glass: Boysenberry and cassis lifted by mint and eucalyptus, with cedar, bay leaf and a twist of citrus peel; firm, dusty tannin, lively acidity and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Released with years already on it, it keeps opening for a decade or two, and strong vintages last for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The Oakville vineyard, named for one of the couple who owned it; nothing to do with the island off Massachusetts.
The vineyard's American Viticultural Area, printed with the Napa Valley appellation that contains it.
The house that makes and bottles the wine at St Helena, though the vineyard lies at Oakville.

records.table: Mint and eucalyptus over cassis mark Martha's Vineyard, the Cabernet Sauvignon Heitz Cellar has bottled under that Oakville vineyard's name since the 1966 vintage. It reaches the list with years of age already on it and asks only a gentle decanting.
records.story: Before he had his own cellar, Joe Heitz, who died in 2000, learned his trade in the 1950s as assistant to André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994) at Beaulieu, then taught winemaking at Fresno State. In 1961, with his wife, he bought a small vineyard and winery south of St Helena, and in 1964 the family moved to Spring Valley in the hills east of the town, to a property with a stone cellar of 1898. The early wines were bought in cask and bottled under the Heitz name. In 1965 Heitz agreed on a handshake to take every Cabernet grape from an Oakville vineyard a couple had bought two years before; that first crop went into his regular bottling. From the 1966 vintage he bottled it apart under the vineyard's name, Martha's Vineyard, and the house calls it the first Napa wine labelled by vineyard. The 1970 stood among the California reds at the Paris tasting of 1976. Phylloxera later killed the old vines and the vineyard was replanted, so no Martha's Vineyard was made from the vintages 1993 to 1995. The family sold the winery in 2018. Martha's Vineyard made a Napa vineyard's name worth reading on a label, and its mint is a cue blind tasters learn early.

Joe Heitz's year of birth (1919) was found only by inference from an obituary's age, so he is dated by his death in 2000 (the house, Decanter); his years at Beaulieu, about 1951 to 1958, and Fresno State rest on Decanter and The Wine Cellar Insider.
The founder's wife and the couple who bought the vineyard in 1963 are described, not named, since whether each is living was not settled.

The barrel time carries no figure: the house's 2013 sheet gives a year in neutral tanks, then new Limousin oak and a year in bottle, while its 2014 sheet gives four years in French oak vessels of many sizes and two in bottle.
That Martha's Vineyard was the first Napa wine labelled by vineyard is the house's claim; the plan's why and the library say among the first, so the record hedges it.

The library's traps p-heitz-cellar and w-marthas-vineyard say the May family farm the vineyard and Heitz does not own it; that speaks of the present and was not tested after the sale of 2018, so the record says only that Heitz bought the grapes from 1965.
Vanity Fair (1985) says an earlier owner planted the first vines and sold before the first crop; with one source the record leaves the planting out.

records.place: Stags Leap District, Napa Valley, California

wine.name: Cask 23 Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, nearly all of it; some years add a touch of another Bordeaux grape, such as Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: A selection from the estate's two Stags Leap District vineyards: S.L.V., planted in 1970, and FAY, first planted to Cabernet in 1961. Vines on volcanic soils on the eastern hillsides give structure; those on the alluvial lower ground give perfume and fruit.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel tanks, with a small part in new French oak barrels in some years, and taken through the malolactic fermentation. The wine is then aged about twenty months in French oak barrels, all or nearly all of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Violet, black cherry and cassis over cedar, cocoa and a hint of sage, with silky, fine tannin that grips gently and a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to enjoy within a few years of release, it gains savoury depth over a decade and keeps for twenty years and more in strong vintages.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for the large wooden cask that held the one lot set apart in 1974.
The winery, written with an apostrophe; the district's name, Stags Leap, carries none.
The wider appellation the wine carries; both vineyards lie in its Stags Leap District.

records.table: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars draws Cask 23, a perfumed, silky Cabernet Sauvignon of violet and black cherry, from its two Stags Leap District vineyards, S.L.V. and FAY. Remember that the Paris winner of 1976 was the house's 1973, not Cask 23.
records.story: A neighbour's wine came first: in the late 1960s Warren Winiarski (1928 to 2024), a Chicago born winemaker, tasted the homemade Cabernet of a grower who in 1961, by the house's account, had planted the first Cabernet Sauvignon in what became the Stags Leap District. In 1970 he bought the ranch next door and planted it as Stag's Leap Vineyard, S.L.V., and the first vintage followed in 1972. On 24 May 1976 the house's 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon, from S.L.V. fruit, took first place among the reds at a blind tasting of French and California wines before French judges in Paris, ahead of Château Mouton Rothschild 1970. Cask 23 began with the harvest of 1974: tasting the young lots with André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), the house found one from S.L.V. so distinct that it was bottled apart and named for the large wooden cask that held it. In 1986 Winiarski bought the grower's vineyard and named it FAY in his honour, and from the 1990 vintage Cask 23 blended the two; by the house's count, that 1990 was only the tenth Cask 23. In 2007 Ste. Michelle Wine Estates and the Antinori family of Florence bought the winery from its founder. With Cask 23 the house gives its own reply to the question Paris asked in 1976.

The founder's dates rest on Decanter (dead in June 2024, aged 95) and a Legacy.com memorial (1928 to 2024); he is dead and named as the house's founder.
The grower who planted FAY in 1961 is described, not named, since his dates were not found in two sources.
The 1974 origin of Cask 23 rests on the house's pages and The Wine Cellar Insider; one merchant calls the vessel a barrel, the house a large wooden cask, and the record follows the house.
The house's brand timeline says the Antinori family took the whole in 2023; the record stops at the sale of 2007 and names no present owner.

The library's trap on w-cask-23 that Cask 23 is not made every vintage rests on its early years (ten in twenty one by 1990, by the house's own letter); whether any year has been skipped since was not found, so the record tells it as history.
The fermentation in steel and the twenty months in new French oak are the house's sheets for 2009 to 2023; the 2023 sheet gives Cabernet Franc as the only other grape, so Merlot is not named.

story: tasted a homemade Cabernet in 1969 becomes in the late 1960s; Grape Collective gives the visit as about 1969 and the wine as a 1968, the Napa Valley Register a 1968, another account a 1969.

open: The house's page calls the 1990 the first Cask 23 to include Fay grapes, and a merchant says the same; whether Fay fruit was bought for any lot before 1986 was not found.

The first Cabernet of the district, planted in 1961, is in Wine Spectator's obituary of the grower, the Napa Valley Wine Academy and a district guide beside the house, which answers the lint's note; the hedge stays.
The fermentation in steel with a small share in new barrels rests on the house's sheets of 2012 to 2016; the sheets of 2022 and 2023 met here name no vessel.

wine.name: Chateau Montelena Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, from vineyards across the Napa Valley.
wine.sites: Vineyards across the Napa Valley, as the appellation on the label says; the estate's own vineyards at Calistoga give its Cabernet Sauvignon. The Paris wine of 1973 drew most of its fruit from Sonoma County, with the rest from Napa.
wine.making: Made without the malolactic fermentation, as Mike Grgich made the 1973, so the wine keeps its crisp malic acidity and takes on no buttery note. It is then aged about ten months in French oak barrels, a small share of them new.
wine.glass: Green apple, white peach and lemon zest over wet stone and a light touch of toasted hazelnut, with bright acidity, no buttery richness and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Fresh and taut on release, it rounds out over five to ten years, and strong vintages keep for a decade and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The estate, its name a contraction of Mount Saint Helena, the peak above Calistoga.
The appellation: the grapes may come from anywhere in the valley, not only the estate.
The grape, the same that won the white flight in Paris with the 1973.

records.table: The white flight in Paris in 1976 went to Chateau Montelena's 1973 Chardonnay. Made without malolactic fermentation, as the 1973 was, the wine is crisp and taut, green apple and white peach rather than butter, a Napa white with Burgundy's restraint.
records.story: At the foot of Mount Saint Helena, north of Calistoga, Alfred L. Tubbs (1827 to 1896), a San Francisco rope maker, acquired land in 1882; he planted vines and built the stone château, and by his death the winery stood among the valley's large ones. His grandson revived it after Prohibition, in 1933, and in 1958 the family sold the château to a couple who dug Jade Lake and laid out a Chinese garden around it. In 1972 Jim Barrett (1926 to 2013) and his partners bought the estate and hired Mike Grgich (1923 to 2023) to make the wine. Grgich bought grapes for the 1973 Chardonnay, most of them from Sonoma County, and blocked its malolactic fermentation. When French judges tasted it blind in Paris on 24 May 1976, it came first among the whites, ahead of a Meursault Charmes, while Stag's Leap Wine Cellars won the reds; a bottle of it went to the Smithsonian. Grgich left in 1977 to found his own winery. For a sommelier the Chardonnay is the bottle a guest names, because it carries the Paris story, while the estate's own Cabernet is the wine of its Calistoga vineyards.

others.name: Montelena Estate Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The estate's own Calistoga Cabernet, built for long ageing: the wine of the vineyard rather than of the Paris story.

others.name: Chateau Montelena Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon

traps: Montelena won Paris with Chardonnay; the red flight went to Stag's Leap Wine Cellars.
The 1973 that won in Paris was made mostly from Sonoma County grapes, not from the Calistoga estate.
The château dates from the 1880s, but the wine of the Paris story came only after the revival of 1972.

cards.front: Who made the 1973 Chardonnay that won the white flight in Paris in 1976?

questions.q: A guest who dislikes buttery Chardonnay asks about Chateau Montelena. Why does it taste crisp rather than buttery?
opts: It is made without malolactic fermentation
It is aged only in stainless steel
It comes from Carneros vineyards alone
It is blended with Sauvignon Blanc
questions.exp: Montelena leaves out the malolactic fermentation, which would turn malic acid into softer lactic acid and bring a buttery note; the wine spends months in French oak all the same, so it is not a steel aged wine.

questions.q: Most of the grapes in the 1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay that won in Paris came from where?
opts: Sonoma County vineyards
The estate at Calistoga
The Carneros district
Oakville on the valley floor
questions.exp: Grgich bought most of the fruit in Sonoma County, in the Alexander and Russian River valleys, with the rest from Napa; the estate's own vineyards gave only a small share.

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35, three restricted to montelena.com; no fetch tried.

Dates: Tubbs (1827 to 1896) on Wikipedia's Alfred L. Tubbs and the Wine History Project; Jim Barrett (1926 to 2013) on Wikipedia and the Associated Press obituary (dead in March 2013 aged 86); Mike Grgich (1923 to 2023) on the Boston Globe obituary (dead in December 2023 aged 100) and a 2013 report of him at 90 in April.

The Sonoma share of the 1973 differs by source: the house's breakdown of 2014 (Belle Terre, Bacigalupi, Hanna in Oak Knoll and a little Calistoga) makes it about three quarters, the Houston Chronicle 85 per cent; the record says most.
Who gave the name Chateau Montelena, and when (1934 or 1940), is disputed, so the story leaves the renaming out and the label gives only the contraction (Wikipedia, the Wine Cellar Insider).

The ten months in French oak and the small new share are the house's sheets for 2022 and 2023 (about a quarter new); the vineyards of the present Chardonnay were not found, so the sites name no district.
The Franks of 1958 are described, not named; their origin differs by source, and they made no wine, by Wikipedia's account.
The library's p-chateau-montelena agrees on every point tested; its trap that Calistoga became an AVA long after was not tested.

changed: story: but by the end of the Second World War the family had stopped making wine is cut; one summary of this check says the winery closed again on the grandson's death in 1947, so the war as the end is wrong, and with one source the year of 1947 is not added.

wine.sites: the 1973's fruit from Napa becomes the rest, no longer a little; the house's breakdown, as the author reports it, puts about a quarter in Napa (Hanna in Oak Knoll and a little Calistoga), and the Napa Wine Project says only the majority came from Sonoma.
open: The shares of the 1973: Belle Terre and Bacigalupi about three quarters by the house's breakdown, one account placing Bacigalupi wrongly in Oak Knoll, the Houston Chronicle 85 per cent; most stays.
The stone château is of about 1888 in the National Register's listing, 1886 and 1884 in other accounts; the story gives no year and says only that Tubbs built it.
Grgich's leaving in 1977 to found his own winery and the dates of Barrett and Grgich were not searched again; they rest on the author's obituaries and the library.

wine.name: Opus One
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, much the larger part, with Petit Verdot, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and a touch of Malbec, the shares shifting with the year.
wine.sites: Four estate parcels in the west of Oakville: two within the old To Kalon vineyard, and the Ballestra and River parcels around the winery. Alluvial soils at the foot of the Mayacamas, the gravel giving way to clay and silt towards the Napa River.
wine.making: The blocks are judged lot by lot, the soils of each helping decide what goes to Opus One and what to Overture. The chosen wine spends about a year and a half in new French oak barrels, is bottled, and rests more than a year in bottle at the winery before its release each October.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black cherry and cassis with cocoa, cedar and a touch of violet; polished rather than powerful, with fine, ripe tannin, fresh acidity and a long, even finish.
wine.ageing: Supple on release, it opens fully after eight to ten years in a strong vintage and keeps for two decades and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: From the musical opus, a composer's work: the name the two founders gave their joint wine.
The appellation Opus One carries, wider than Oakville, where the estate's vineyards lie.

records.table: Robert Mondavi and Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Mouton went into partnership to make Opus One, an Oakville red whose first vintage was the 1979. Cabernet Sauvignon leads the other Bordeaux grapes in a polished wine with fine grained tannin.
records.story: Hawaii was where the two founders first met, in 1970: Robert Mondavi (1913 to 2008), of the Robert Mondavi Winery at Oakville, and Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988), of Château Mouton Rothschild in Pauillac. In 1978, at Mouton, they agreed to make one wine together: a Napa red on the pattern of Bordeaux. The first vintage, the 1979, was made at the Robert Mondavi Winery, the partnership was announced in 1980, and the 1979 and 1980 were released together in 1984. The name borrows the musical opus, a composer's work. The Baron died in 1988 and his daughter carried the partnership on. Ground was broken for the estate's own winery in 1989, and it was finished in October 1991, in time for that year's harvest; until then every vintage had been made at the Mondavi winery. In 2004 the Mondavi company was bought by Constellation Brands, and its half of Opus One went with it. Overture, the estate's second wine, takes the lots not chosen for the grand vin. Opus One joined a Bordeaux first growth and Napa in one name; open it for a guest curious how the two meet.

others.name: Overture
others.note: The estate's second wine, first made in 1993 from lots not chosen for Opus One; long sold without a vintage, it first carried one with the 2021.

traps: The Rothschild of Opus One is the Mouton branch of the family, not the Lafite branch.
Opus One is its own winery and wine, not a bottling of the Robert Mondavi Winery, though its first vintages were made there.
The first vintage is 1979, but it reached the market only in 1984, together with the 1980.

report: Searches for this record: nine of the group's 35, four restricted to opusonewinery.com; no fetch tried; the group spent 31 in all.

Dates: Robert Mondavi (1913 to 2008) on Wikipedia and Britannica; Baron Philippe (1902 to 1988) on Wikipedia's Philippe de Rothschild (dead in Paris on 20 January 1988) and the estate's own page (born 1902), with Britannica in the refuted Mouton record of bordeaux-left.
The bordeaux-left Mouton record describes the Napa partner rather than naming him, his dates not then found in two sources; they are found here, so the integrator may name him there.

The first meeting in Hawaii in 1970 rests on Wikipedia and Wine Spectator (eight years before the meeting at Mouton in 1978); Decanter says the plan was first discussed in 1973, so the story says only that they first met in 1970.
The library's w-opus-one calls Overture the non vintage second wine; the estate's own pages list an Overture 2021, so the record says it has since carried a vintage.

The library's 'first serious joint venture between a First Growth proprietor and a New World producer' was not tested, and the record makes no claim of a first; the architect of 1991 and the launch price of 1984 are left out.

The barrel time (seventeen to nineteen months, by vintage) and the fifteen months in bottle before an October release are the estate's own pages; founded is the library's 1979, the first vintage, though the partners agreed in 1978.

changed: wine.making: rests about fifteen months more becomes rests more than a year in bottle; two merchants give fifteen months and a release on the first of October, one guide eighteen months, one merchant's 2012 sheet a year and a half.
